resources.title: California quail
resources.description: Identify California quail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: California quail (Callipepla californica): 9.4-10.6 in; plump quail with a forward-curving black topknot. White streaks on gray-brown sides and a heavily scaled pattern on the belly. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: A permanent resident of the Pacific coast states and parts of the interior West; common along the California coast and present in the Northwest, Rocky Mountain and Southwest regions, including introduced populations.

rangeSummary.value: A permanent resident of the Pacific coast states and parts of the interior West; common along the California coast and present in the Northwest, Rocky Mountain and Southwest regions, including introduced populations.

identification.text: 9.4-10.6 in; plump quail with a forward-curving black topknot.
White streaks on gray-brown sides and a heavily scaled pattern on the belly.
Call a loud 'chi-CA-go', the second note highest.
Compared with the gambel's quail: Replaces California quail in desert country; compare carefully where ranges meet.
Compared with the mountain quail: Mountain quail lives mostly at higher elevations and has broad white bars on reddish sides.

habitat.text: Broken chaparral, woodland edges, coastal scrub, open oak woodland and streamside growth; also suburbs, farms, pinyon-juniper and grassland edges.
Avoids mountains; introduced birds farther inland use other brushy habitats.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Lives in coveys most of the year; often seen strutting across clearings, nodding at each step, and flushes in fast, low, whirring flight.
Forages on the ground by scratching and picking; eats mainly seeds and leaves, also acorns, berries, bulbs and insects.
Permanent resident; comes into well-covered yards and parks for grain or birdseed.

resources.title: Chukar
resources.description: Identify Chukar, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Chukar (Alectoris chukar): Rotund partridge with sandy-brown upperparts, gray breast and buff belly. Bold black band across the forehead and through the eye forming a necklace around a white or creamy throat. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to Eurasia. Introduced and resident in western North America from British Columbia, northern Idaho and central and eastern Montana south to Nevada, northern Arizona, northwestern New Mexico and south-central Colorado; also established in Hawaii.

rangeSummary.value: Native to Eurasia. Introduced and resident in western North America from British Columbia, northern Idaho and central and eastern Montana south to Nevada, northern Arizona, northwestern New Mexico and south-central Colorado; also established in Hawaii.

identification.text: Rotund partridge with sandy-brown upperparts, gray breast and buff belly.
Bold black band across the forehead and through the eye forming a necklace around a white or creamy throat.
Flanks boldly barred black, white and chestnut.
Coral-red bill, legs and eye-ring; short tail with chestnut outer feathers.
Juveniles are duller and mottled, lacking the sharp head and flank pattern.

habitat.text: Rocky, grassy or brushy slopes in arid mountains and canyons, often grassland mixed with sagebrush or saltbush; introduced cheatgrass is a key element; needs water unless green leaves are plentiful.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Travels in coveys from late summer to early spring
Territorial males give a harsh cackling chuk chuk chukar from rocky cliffs in spring
Feeds mostly on the ground on seeds and leaves (including cheatgrass and Russian thistle seed), berries and, in spring and summer, insects
Permanent resident in its North American range

resources.title: Dusky grouse
resources.description: Identify Dusky grouse, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Dusky grouse (Dendragapus obscurus): Male: uniformly gray and dark, with reddish bare neck patches ringed in white feathers visible during courtship. Female: mottled brown and gray. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Western North America: Rocky Mountains and interior West from Alaska, Yukon and western Canada south to the US Southwest.

rangeSummary.value: Western North America: Rocky Mountains and interior West from Alaska, Yukon and western Canada south to the US Southwest.

identification.text: Male: uniformly gray and dark, with reddish bare neck patches ringed in white feathers visible during courtship.
Female: mottled brown and gray.
Over most of the range, dark tail with a broad gray tip.
Crow- to mallard-sized.
Compared with the sooty grouse: Recently split from the dusky grouse; the two were formerly combined as 'blue grouse'.

habitat.text: Deciduous and mixed mountain forest in summer, especially where forest meets open country such as sagebrush flats; higher-elevation conifer forest in winter.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Males give a series of deep hoots in the breeding season, increasing in tempo and volume.
Slow-moving and inconspicuous but often surprisingly tame.
Feeds on the ground in summer and in trees in winter, especially in deep snow.
Unusual uphill altitudinal migration: moves up into dense conifer forest in autumn, up to about 30 miles.

resources.title: Gambel's quail
resources.description: Identify Gambel's quail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Gambel's quail (Callipepla gambelii): Curving teardrop topknot on the head. White stripes on chestnut-red sides. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Desert Southwest of the United States, centred on the Sonoran Desert. Not found in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Desert Southwest of the United States, centred on the Sonoran Desert. Not found in Canada.

identification.text: Curving teardrop topknot on the head.
White stripes on chestnut-red sides.
Male: reddish cap and a black patch in the centre of a yellowish belly.
Female: redder on the sides than a female California quail, with a less scaly belly pattern.
Compared with the california quail: The female Gambel's quail is redder on the sides with a less scaly belly than the female California quail.

habitat.text: Brushy Sonoran desert and canyons with open ground, varied shrubs, cactus and mesquite thickets, concentrated near water. Avoids unbroken grassland without shrubs; can be common in open suburbs.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Coveys walk to water in the morning and evening, giving clucking and crowing notes; call is a ringing 'puk-kwaw-cah'.
Forages in flocks from late summer to early spring, mostly on the ground but also in shrubs for berries, leaves and buds.
Coveys roost at night in bushes or low trees.
Mostly vegetarian: seeds, shoots, leaves, cactus fruit and berries such as mistletoe and hackberry.

resources.title: Greater prairie-chicken
resources.description: Identify Greater prairie-chicken, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Greater prairie-chicken (Tympanuchus cupido): Chunky brown grouse, 41-48 cm, heavily barred, especially on the underparts. Short black tail visible in flight. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Now uncommon and localized to remaining native tall-grass prairie in the midwestern United States. The Atlantic Coast race (Heath Hen) became extinct in 1932 and the Texas coastal Attwater's race is seriously endangered.

rangeSummary.value: Now uncommon and localized to remaining native tall-grass prairie in the midwestern United States. The Atlantic Coast race (Heath Hen) became extinct in 1932 and the Texas coastal Attwater's race is seriously endangered.

identification.text: Chunky brown grouse, 41-48 cm, heavily barred, especially on the underparts.
Short black tail visible in flight.
Male has yellow-orange neck air sacs and raised feather tufts, visible only in courtship display.
Sexes similar; male slightly larger.

habitat.text: Native tall-grass prairie, including prairie interspersed with agricultural fields; prime original habitat was prairie mixed with oak woodland. Nests on the ground in thick tall grass.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: In spring, typically 8-20 males gather on 'booming grounds', often a low hill with good visibility, and display with a hollow moaning 'boom', foot-stamping and cackles.
Some birds are permanent residents; others move up to about 160 km (100 miles) between breeding and wintering areas.
Forages mostly on the ground, mainly in early morning and evening; winter diet is leaves, seeds and waste grain, summer diet adds buds, berries and insects.

conservationStatus.text: Attwater's greater prairie-chicken (Tympanuchus cupido attwateri): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1967-03-11.

resources.title: Greater sage-grouse
resources.description: Identify Greater sage-grouse, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Greater sage-grouse (Centrocercus urophasianus): Large grouse with a long, spiky tail. Male: white breast contrasting with a black bib and black belly; two yellow air sacs inflated in display. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Sagebrush regions of the western US and western Canada; it has disappeared from much of its former range.

rangeSummary.value: Sagebrush regions of the western US and western Canada; it has disappeared from much of its former range.

identification.text: Large grouse with a long, spiky tail.
Male: white breast contrasting with a black bib and black belly; two yellow air sacs inflated in display.
Female: plainer, told by large size, long tail and dark belly patch.
Compared with the gunnison sage-grouse: Gunnison is smaller, with bolder pale tail bars, a longer head plume and a different display; their ranges do not overlap.

habitat.text: Sagebrush plains, high valleys, mesas and foothills; found only near sagebrush and needs access to water.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Males display on traditional leks, puffing the white chest, inflating air sacs and fanning the tail with loud pops and bubbling sounds.
Flushed birds give a chicken-like cackle.
Eats mostly sagebrush leaves and shoots, plus flowers, buds and summer insects.
Largely non-migratory, with local movements out of high valleys in winter.

resources.title: Gunnison sage-grouse
resources.description: Identify Gunnison sage-grouse, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Gunnison sage-grouse (Centrocercus minimus): Smaller than the greater sage-grouse. More obvious pale bars on the tail feathers and a longer plume on the back of the head. Do not shoot unless you are certain of the species. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Year-round resident of southwestern Colorado and adjacent Utah only; gone from about 90 percent of its former range.

rangeSummary.value: Year-round resident of southwestern Colorado and adjacent Utah only; gone from about 90 percent of its former range.

identification.text: Smaller than the greater sage-grouse.
More obvious pale bars on the tail feathers and a longer plume on the back of the head.
Displaying males puff out a white chest and inflate yellow air sacs; males slightly larger than females.
Compared with the greater sage-grouse: Greater is larger, with a different display and fainter tail bars; the ranges do not overlap.

habitat.text: Sagebrush plains and high valleys; nesting habitat includes lower wet areas where young forage for insects.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Displaying male gives 9–10 low hooting gobbles with wing sounds, very different from the greater sage-grouse display.
Fall and winter diet may be almost entirely sagebrush leaves and shoots; also flowers, buds and summer insects.

conservationStatus.text: Listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act by the 2014 final rule.
Colorado sets no season and no bag limit for Gunnison sage-grouse.
The gunnison sage-grouse, wherever found: listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 2014-12-22.

resources.title: Lesser prairie-chicken
resources.description: Identify Lesser prairie-chicken, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Lesser prairie-chicken (Tympanuchus pallidicinctus): 15-20 in; grouse barred brown and buff, paler and slightly smaller than Greater Prairie-Chicken. Displaying male shows purplish (not yellow) neck sacs. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Great Plains of the United States (Plains, Southwest and Texas regions); now uncommon and found in a few local concentrations after serious decline.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Great Plains of the United States (Plains, Southwest and Texas regions); now uncommon and found in a few local concentrations after serious decline.

identification.text: 15-20 in; grouse barred brown and buff, paler and slightly smaller than Greater Prairie-Chicken.
Displaying male shows purplish (not yellow) neck sacs.
Best told from Greater Prairie-Chicken by range, since they do not overlap.
Compared with the greater prairie-chicken: Greater is larger and darker with yellow-orange neck sacs and does not share the Lesser's range.

habitat.text: Sandy short-grass prairie with sand sage and bluestem, often near low shinnery (shin) oak stands.
Visits grain fields but disappears where too much native prairie is converted to farmland.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Males give a booming call on courtship display grounds; otherwise cackling and clucking notes.
May move several miles daily from roosts to feeding sites; no regular migration, though some shift between summer and winter ranges.
Eats seeds and leaves, oak leaves and acorns, waste grain in fall and winter, and many grasshoppers and beetles in summer.

resources.title: Montezuma quail
resources.description: Identify Montezuma quail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Montezuma quail (Cyrtonyx montezumae): 8-10 in; small, chunky quail with a puffy, rounded head. Male: bold clownish black-and-white face pattern and many white spots on a chestnut belly. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: In the United States found only in the Mexican border region of the Southwest and Texas.

rangeSummary.value: In the United States found only in the Mexican border region of the Southwest and Texas.

identification.text: 8-10 in; small, chunky quail with a puffy, rounded head.
Male: bold clownish black-and-white face pattern and many white spots on a chestnut belly.
Female: pale brown and subtly marked, but has the same head shape.
Call a soft, descending whinny.

habitat.text: Grassy oak canyons and wooded mountain slopes with bunchgrass; needs tall grass and usually oaks.
Open oak or pine-oak woodland and grassy hills with scattered trees; avoids low deserts.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Crouches motionless until nearly stepped on, then explodes into whirring flight.
Fall and winter coveys usually under ten birds, often using a very small area.
Digs in soil with its feet for bulbs (wood sorrel, nutgrass) and scratches leaf litter under oaks for insects, acorns and seeds.
Mostly resident; northern birds may move to lower elevations in winter.

resources.title: Mountain quail
resources.description: Identify Mountain quail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Mountain quail (Oreortyx pictus): Two long thin head plumes, often combined into one, standing straight up. Blue-gray head and chest with a chestnut face. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Mountains of the western United States from southern Washington and western Idaho south through the Cascades and Sierra Nevada into Baja California, at about 450–3,000 m. May have disappeared from southwestern British Columbia, where it was possibly introduced.

rangeSummary.value: Mountains of the western United States from southern Washington and western Idaho south through the Cascades and Sierra Nevada into Baja California, at about 450–3,000 m. May have disappeared from southwestern British Columbia, where it was possibly introduced.

identification.text: Two long thin head plumes, often combined into one, standing straight up.
Blue-gray head and chest with a chestnut face.
Broad white bars on chestnut sides.
Sexes similar; 26–28 cm.

habitat.text: Dense brush in wooded foothills and mountains, especially pine-oak woodland, coniferous forest and chaparral; uses post-fire or clearcut brush; seldom more than about a mile from water in hot weather.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Coveys keep to dense cover and often sit motionless when approached
Males give a loud echoing kyork or woook at long intervals in spring
High-elevation birds migrate downslope on foot for winter
Scratches in litter and digs for bulbs; eats seeds, acorns, leaves, berries, some insects and fungi

resources.title: Northern bobwhite
resources.description: Identify Northern bobwhite, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern bobwhite (Colinus virginianus): Small, chunky quail, 20-28 cm, with a reddish-brown body and very short tail. Contrasting pale eyebrow and throat: white on the male, buff on the female. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: The only native quail in eastern North America, resident from southern Eastern Canada and the Great Lakes through the eastern and central United States to Florida and Texas, and south to Guatemala. It has disappeared from much of the northern part of its range; the masked race is being reintroduced in southern Arizona.

rangeSummary.value: The only native quail in eastern North America, resident from southern Eastern Canada and the Great Lakes through the eastern and central United States to Florida and Texas, and south to Guatemala. It has disappeared from much of the northern part of its range; the masked race is being reintroduced in southern Arizona.

identification.text: Small, chunky quail, 20-28 cm, with a reddish-brown body and very short tail.
Contrasting pale eyebrow and throat: white on the male, buff on the female.
Male of the endangered 'masked bobwhite' race of the Southwest has a black face and rusty chest.
Compared with the meadowlarks: Audubon lists meadowlarks among other chunky field birds to compare; the bobwhite has a very short tail and a bold pale eyebrow and throat.

habitat.text: Semi-open farmland and brushy country: brushy meadows, overgrown fields, roadsides and wood edges, and pastures or fields next to hedgerows or woodlots. The masked race uses ungrazed native grassland.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Heard more often than seen; the whistled 'bob-white!' is a familiar spring call.
Lives in coveys averaging about a dozen birds in fall and winter; coveys roost on the ground in a circle, tails in and heads out.
Forages by walking with head down, eating seeds (especially legumes), leaves, buds, berries, acorns and insects.
Permanent resident; does not migrate.

conservationStatus.text: Masked bobwhite (quail) (Colinus virginianus ridgwayi): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1967-03-11.

resources.title: Scaled quail
resources.description: Identify Scaled quail, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Scaled quail (Callipepla squamata): 10-12 in; blue-gray quail with a fluffy white crest (hence 'cottontop'). Dark edges on gray body feathers create a scaled look. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Permanent resident of the arid southwestern United States: the southern Plains, southern Rockies, Southwest and Texas.

rangeSummary.value: Permanent resident of the arid southwestern United States: the southern Plains, southern Rockies, Southwest and Texas.

identification.text: 10-12 in; blue-gray quail with a fluffy white crest (hence 'cottontop').
Dark edges on gray body feathers create a scaled look.
Sexes very similar; female may have a shorter crest.
Call a low nasal 'pe-cos'.

habitat.text: Flat open country or rolling hills with grasses, annual weeds and scattered shrubs; also grassland grading into desert, juniper slopes and dry brush.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Coveys travel on foot and tend to run rather than fly when disturbed.
Males call from fence posts or rocks in spring; coveys roost on the ground in dense low growth at night.
Eats weed and woody-plant seeds (snakeweed, Russian thistle, mesquite), green leaves and berries, and more insects than most quail.

resources.title: Sooty grouse
resources.description: Identify Sooty grouse, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Sooty grouse (Dendragapus fuliginosus): Male dark slaty gray with a yellow comb and a long blackish tail tipped with a broad pale gray band. In spring display the male shows yellow neck air sacs ringed by white feathers. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Resident from coastal southeastern Alaska and coastal British Columbia (including Haida Gwaii and Vancouver Island) south through the coast ranges and Cascades to northwestern California and the Sierra Nevada.

rangeSummary.value: Resident from coastal southeastern Alaska and coastal British Columbia (including Haida Gwaii and Vancouver Island) south through the coast ranges and Cascades to northwestern California and the Sierra Nevada.

identification.text: Male dark slaty gray with a yellow comb and a long blackish tail tipped with a broad pale gray band.
In spring display the male shows yellow neck air sacs ringed by white feathers.
Female mottled brown and gray.
Large: Alaska's largest upland game bird.
Compared with the dusky grouse: Very similar and separated mainly by range; dusky grouse lives in the interior West.

habitat.text: Coastal and mountain coniferous forest; many birds move in autumn from open breeding areas into dense conifers; coastal birds may use semi-open old-growth or logged forest year-round.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Displaying males give deep, owl-like hoots, often from high in a dense conifer, sometimes audible over a mile away
Slow-moving and often surprisingly tame
Forages on the ground in summer and in trees in winter, eating conifer needles
Hens with broods use muskeg edges, logged areas and roadsides from late June

resources.title: White-tailed ptarmigan
resources.description: Identify White-tailed ptarmigan, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: White-tailed ptarmigan (Lagopus leucura): Smallest North American grouse, 30–33 cm. White tail feathers (hard to see except in flight). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Resident from central Alaska, Yukon and the southwestern Mackenzie south through the mountains of British Columbia, Alberta and Vancouver Island to the Washington Cascades and the Rockies as far as northern New Mexico; introduced in the Sierra Nevada of California and in Oregon and Utah. It is the only ptarmigan south of Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Resident from central Alaska, Yukon and the southwestern Mackenzie south through the mountains of British Columbia, Alberta and Vancouver Island to the Washington Cascades and the Rockies as far as northern New Mexico; introduced in the Sierra Nevada of California and in Oregon and Utah. It is the only ptarmigan south of Canada.

identification.text: Smallest North American grouse, 30–33 cm.
White tail feathers (hard to see except in flight).
Summer plumage mottled brown and gray; winter plumage entirely white except the dark eye and bill.
Feathered legs and feet.
Compared with the other ptarmigan (willow, rock): White-tailed is smaller, has a white rather than black tail and usually lives higher in the mountains.

habitat.text: Rocky alpine tundra above timberline with low vegetation or damp alpine meadows near snowfields; in winter where willows extend above the snow.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current place-, date-, method- and animal-class rules. Library inclusion is not evidence of legal opportunity.

behavior.text: Crouches motionless when approached and is easily overlooked
Feeds in flocks from late summer through winter, nipping buds, twigs and leaves of willow and other low alpine plants
Moves to slightly lower elevations in winter, some up to 14 miles; females move farther than males

conservationStatus.text: Mt. Rainier white-tailed ptarmigan (Lagopus leucura rainierensis): listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 2024-08-02.

content.plainText: Sage-grouse seasons, where they exist, are set for greater sage-grouse in specific areas. Check the responsible authority's map and species before hunting near the Gunnison range, and if you are not certain which species you are looking at, do not shoot.
